title: How long can you last?
principle: Businesses die when cash runs out, not when profit does.

screens.text: Let me start with a story. In December 2018, Jet Airways had 119 planes flying across India. Four months later, not one of them could take off. Before I tell you why, have a guess.

screens.prompt: What do you think grounded an airline that big?
screens.why: It simply ran out of cash. Most people guess something dramatic, but the real reason was ordinary: Jet couldn't pay for fuel, and its pilots hadn't been paid for months.

screens.title: The slow leak
screens.text: Now you know what happened, but how does a huge airline actually run out of cash? Month after month, more money went out than came in. Fuel, salaries and plane rent all had to be paid, the ticket money wasn't enough, and so Jet's pile of cash kept shrinking.

screens.title: Your runway
screens.text: Think of the cash in a bank as petrol in a tank, and a monthly loss as a leak in that tank. The one number I want you to know is how many months are left before the tank runs dry. That number is your runway.

screens.prompt: Let's try one. A business has ₹30 lakh in the bank and loses ₹5 lakh every month. How long is its runway?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹30 lakh divided by ₹5 lakh is 6 months, and that's the whole runway sum: the cash you have, divided by the cash you lose each month. If nothing changes, this owner has six months to fix the business or find more money.

wrong.a: Close. Let me show you the sum: ₹30 lakh divided by ₹5 lakh is 6, so if nothing changes, the cash lasts 6 months.
wrong.c: Not quite. ₹30 lakh is the cash you have, not the number of months. Divide it by the ₹5 lakh lost each month, and you get 6 months.

screens.prompt: Jet's cash was running low, so it asked its banks for ₹400 crore. Why might a bank still say no?

options.label: The losses hadn't stopped, so the loan would burn too
₹400 crore was too small to matter

screens.why: Exactly. ₹400 crore could buy Jet more time, but it wouldn't fix the leak, and with the losses still running, the new money would vanish too. The banks said no, and on 17 April 2019 Jet flew its last flight.

wrong.a: Banks do lend to airlines. But think like the lender for a moment: what happens after I hand you the money? If the business keeps losing cash, my loan disappears with it.
wrong.c: ₹400 crore could pay for a lot of fuel and wages. The bigger question was what came after, because if Jet kept losing cash, the new money would only buy a little time.

screens.title: From their story to yours
screens.text: Jet's story has crores and planes, but the same leak quietly closes small shops every day, and most owners never see it coming. So let's shrink it to your size. Say you've opened a small gym, and let's find out how long your money would last.

screens.prompt: Your gym has ₹3 lakh in the bank. ₹1.5 lakh goes out each month, and members pay you ₹1 lakh. What's your runway?
screens.why: Well done. ₹1.5 lakh goes out, but ₹1 lakh comes back in, so your cash only shrinks by ₹50,000 a month. That means ₹3 lakh gives you 6 months of runway.

wrong.a: I see what you did: ₹3 lakh divided by ₹1.5 lakh. But your members still pay you ₹1 lakh, so your real monthly loss is only ₹50,000, and your runway is 6 months.
wrong.b: You're close, but find the gap first. ₹1.5 lakh out minus ₹1 lakh in leaves a loss of ₹50,000 a month, and ₹3 lakh divided by ₹50,000 gives you 6 months.

screens.prompt: Your gym has ₹3 lakh and loses ₹50,000 a month. Which of these stretches your runway the most?

options.label: Put ₹50,000 more into the bank, once
Sign 10 new members at ₹1,000 a month

screens.why: Exactly. Your monthly loss falls from ₹50,000 to ₹25,000, so the same ₹3 lakh now lasts 12 months. Notice that you didn't add any petrol. You made the leak smaller, so every rupee already in the tank goes further.

wrong.b: That does help, since ₹3.5 lakh divided by ₹50,000 gives you 7 months. But next month the same leak carries on. Cutting ₹25,000 of costs shrinks the leak every month and gives you 12.
wrong.c: That's useful too. Ten members bring in ₹10,000 more, so your loss falls to ₹40,000 and you get about 7½ months. Cutting ₹25,000 of costs shrinks the loss further and gives you 12.

screens.prompt: Your trainers' ₹20,000 is due on Saturday. I'll show you six things. For each one, tell me: can you spend it today?

items.text: A company promising 20 memberships next month
₹30,000 a member owes you, due in 60 days

screens.why: Exactly. The ₹8,000 by UPI and the ₹12,000 in your account make the ₹20,000 you need. The other things may be worth money someday, but you can't spend them this Saturday, and runway only counts cash you can use.

screens.setup: Then a big chance arrives. A local company wants memberships for 40 staff, worth ₹40,000 a month. But you'd need ₹1.5 lakh of new machines first, and the company usually pays only after three months.
screens.question: You have 6 months of runway. How do you chase this deal without risking the gym?

options.label: Say yes and buy the machines today
options.outcome: Your bank falls from ₹3 lakh to ₹1.5 lakh overnight, and your old ₹50,000 loss carries on each month. By the time the company's first payment is due, that ₹1.5 lakh is gone.
options.why: The deal makes money later, but the cash leaves much earlier, and that's the trap. Before saying yes to a big order, ask what happens to your bank balance before the customer pays.
options.better: Ask for the first three months in advance, or rent the machines.

options.label: Say yes, if they pay three months up front
options.outcome: They pay ₹1.2 lakh up front, which is three months of fees, so the machines take only ₹30,000 of your own cash. After that, ₹40,000 a month comes in, and your monthly gap shrinks from ₹50,000 to ₹10,000.
options.why: Well played. You changed when the cash arrives, not what the deal is worth, so the advance paid for the machines instead of your ₹3 lakh.

options.label: Say no. It's too risky
options.outcome: You keep your ₹3 lakh, but the ₹50,000 monthly loss carries on, your runway stays at 6 months, and the company takes the deal to another gym.
options.why: That's safer than spending blindly, but there was a better move: change the payment terms before giving up the deal.
options.better: Ask for an advance before you say no.

screens.text: A business doesn't shut when its profit runs out. It shuts when its ___ runs out, and the months it has left are its ___.
screens.why: Exactly. In April 2019, Jet still had its planes and its loyal flyers, but none of that could pay for that day's fuel and wages. When usable cash hits zero, a business can stop while it still owns valuable things, and that's why I want you watching your runway.

summary: Your runway is how many months your cash lasts: cash in the bank ÷ monthly loss.
Count only the gap between money out and money in.
Fixing the leak beats topping up the tank, and every big deal should be checked against your runway.

cards.front: You make ₹20,000 profit a month, but buyers pay in 90 days. What should you watch most?
options: Cash in the bank each week
cards.back: Cash. Profit that arrives in 90 days can't pay this week's bills.

cards.front: ₹2,40,000 in the bank. You lose ₹40,000 a month. How long can you last?
A big new order pays in 90 days. What makes it safe?
cards.back: Bring the cash closer. Growth on long credit empties the bank.
